name: ocproxy
desc: User-level SOCKS and port forwarding proxy
why: Userspace TCP/IP stack that tunnels through OpenConnect VPNs without root, a clever way to take a network stack apart.

brief.what_it_is: ocproxy is a user-level SOCKS5 and port-forwarding proxy for OpenConnect VPNs, built on the lwIP TCP/IP stack. OpenConnect runs it as a script, passing it the tunnel file descriptor, and ocproxy turns that tunnel into a local SOCKS5 server (-D) and local ports that forward over the VPN (-L). Only the connections a user explicitly sends through it go over the VPN, so the VPN no longer captures all host traffic. The optional vpnns companion tool, which is Linux-only and marked experimental, instead runs an application in a separate network namespace attached to the VPN.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says that when using ocproxy, OpenConnect only handles network activity the user specifically asks to proxy, so the VPN interface no longer "hijacks" all network traffic on the host. It also aims at situations where root is unavailable or undesirable, such as multiuser systems, and at connecting to several VPNs at once even when their IP ranges overlap.
brief.how_it_works: OpenConnect is started with --script-tun and --script pointing at ocproxy, which reads its network settings from environment variables set by OpenConnect (INTERNAL_IP4_ADDRESS, INTERNAL_IP4_MTU, INTERNAL_IP4_DNS, CISCO_DEF_DOMAIN) and receives the tunneled traffic on the file descriptor named by VPNFD. Inside the process, lwIP handles the TCP/IP, and the SOCKS5 server and -L forwards open connections over the VPN. The separate vpnns approach creates a fresh user/net/uts/mount namespace with only loopback, then uses --attach to give it a tunnel device, default route and resolv.conf, so no proxy configuration is needed.

commands_seen.context: Main usage: OpenConnect launches ocproxy as its tunnel script, with a SOCKS5 server on 11080 and two forwarded local ports. (The README wraps this across two lines; joined here.)
Connects to a forwarded port, reaching unix-host:22 over the VPN through the -L 2222 mapping.
Uses the SOCKS wrapper socksify to run ssh through the built-in SOCKS5 server.
Same idea using the tsocks wrapper, for a host given by IP address.
One-time setup to create a separate Firefox profile for routing browsing through the VPN.
Runs a second Firefox instance using the previously configured "vpn" profile.
First build step when building ocproxy from git.
Configure step of the build from git; needs libevent >= 2.0, autoconf, automake and gcc.
Experimental vpnns path: connects to an ocserv gateway and hands the tunnel to vpnns inside the namespace.

brief.install_notes: Building from git needs libevent 2.0 or newer (shared library and headers), autoconf, automake, and gcc, binutils and make. The README points to Ubuntu PPA packages for 14.04 LTS and 16.04 LTS (ppa:cernekee, package names ocproxy and openvpn) and says those are needed for the OpenVPN example. OpenConnect should run as a non-root user with ocproxy. vpnns needs Linux kernel 3.8 or newer and an X server that accepts UNIX sockets in /tmp, or a change to /etc/X11/xinit/xserverrc to add -listen unix. Setup for FoxyProxy and tsocks/Dante is per-application configuration.
brief.standout: It runs as a user-space TCP/IP stack under OpenConnect instead of a kernel tun device, so a VPN can serve one application or port without root or touching the host routing table. The companion vpnns tool uses Linux user and network namespaces to do the same job at the whole-application level, with no proxy configuration, and the README says it does not require root or changing host network configuration.
brief.status: unknown. The README has no release dates, changelog, or version numbers. It names Kevin Cernekee as current maintainer and David Edmondson as original author. The Ubuntu 14.04 and 16.04 PPA references look dated. I did not check the commit history or releases page.
brief.caveats: vpnns is marked experimental and is Linux-only; it may interfere with dbus connections. The README notes that OpenVPN support needs out-of-tree patches posted to a mailing list. It requires libevent 2.0+ and a build-from-source path with autotools. Proxy-based use only covers TCP-style apps that can go through SOCKS or a -L forward, and the README says vpnns is better suited to VOIP and BitTorrent. The README does not state a license.
quotes: ocproxy is a user-level SOCKS and port forwarding proxy for OpenConnect based on lwIP.
ocproxy should not be run directly.
When the VPN disconnects, the browser will lose all connectivity, preventing leaks.
Unlike previous approaches to the problem (e.g. anything that involves running `ip netns`), vpnns does not require root privileges or changing the host network configuration.

judge.reason: A user-space TCP/IP stack that turns an OpenConnect tunnel into per-app VPN access without changing host routes is a genuinely unusual networking idea.

entry.title: ocproxy
entry.tldr: A userspace TCP/IP stack that turns an OpenConnect VPN tunnel into a local SOCKS5 server and forwarded ports, with no root and no routing changes.
entry.deeper_look:
ocproxy is a helper for OpenConnect, the open-source client for Cisco AnyConnect-style VPNs. Normally a VPN creates a kernel tunnel device and rewrites the routes, so every program on the machine starts sending traffic through it. ocproxy takes a different path. OpenConnect hands it the tunnel's file descriptor, and ocproxy runs the whole TCP/IP stack inside its own process using lwIP, a small embedded network stack.

The result is a local SOCKS5 server (`-D`) and local ports that forward to hosts on the far side of the VPN (`-L`). Only the connections you point at it go through the tunnel. The rest of the host's traffic never notices. This also works where root is unavailable or unwelcome, such as shared multiuser machines, and it lets you connect to several VPNs at once even when their address ranges overlap.

The idea underneath is that a network stack is just code. It does not have to live in the kernel. Once the packets arrive on a file descriptor, a program can speak TCP, answer DNS, and hand out connections as ordinary sockets. Reading how ocproxy takes its settings from environment variables set by OpenConnect (`INTERNAL_IP4_ADDRESS`, `VPNFD` and others) is a compact lesson in how VPN clients and their scripts talk to each other.

The repository also includes an experimental companion, vpnns. It uses Linux user and network namespaces to run a whole application in its own network world attached to the VPN, so no proxy settings are needed. The README claims it needs no root and no host network changes.
entry.install:
brew install ocproxy
# Also needs OpenConnect and a VPN gateway you can log in to. ocproxy is launched by OpenConnect, not run directly.

try_this.what_happens: OpenConnect starts ocproxy as its tunnel script, opening a SOCKS5 server on port 11080 and forwarding local ports 2222 and 3389 across the VPN.
Connects through the forwarded port to unix-host:22 on the far side of the VPN.
Runs ssh through the built-in SOCKS5 server using the socksify wrapper.

entry.whats_unique: It replaces the kernel tunnel device with a userspace TCP/IP stack, so one application or port can use a VPN without root or touching the host's routes.
entry.caveats: The README shows no release dates and mentions Ubuntu 14.04 and 16.04 packages, so it may be dated; vpnns is Linux-only and marked experimental, and you need a working OpenConnect VPN to try any of it.
